solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Dupe with 35 year-old car at European rally

blocks.note: to dupe is to con
a G-reg car, registered in 1989-90, was about 35 years old when this appeared
taken as written
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone is fooled into bringing an elderly car to a classic-car rally in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: UK number plates once began or ended with a letter showing the year of registration; G covered 1989-90, so a G-reg car was 35 years old in 2024.
explanation.definitionFit: To rally, as a verb, is to come together, which is exactly what people who congregate do.

clue.text: Clever to switch off energy

blocks.note: to cut the power is to switch it off
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone praises the smart idea of turning off the power to save electricity.
explanation.definitionFit: Cute in its older sense means shrewd or ingenious, as in a cute move.

clue.text: New trouble with lawyers limited beauty salon

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
to ail is to trouble or afflict
the Bar is the body of barristers

explanation.surface: A beauty salon run as a limited company runs into fresh legal trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limited' looks like the Ltd of a company name, but it belongs to the definition: a salon limited to doing nails.
explanation.definitionFit: A nail bar is a small salon offering only manicures, so it is a beauty salon with a narrow range of services.

clue.text: Spooner's view of tenant is slightly conservative

indicators.note: Dr Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the phrase that follows is to be said with its initial sounds exchanged

blocks.note: a view is a sight and a tenant is a renter; exchanging the opening sounds of the outer words gives the phrase

explanation.surface: A tenant's outlook on things turns out to be mildly Tory.
explanation.definitionFit: In politics, right-of-centre describes moderate conservative views, leaning right without being extreme.

clue.text: United managers partly like Klopp or Tuchel?

indicators.note: partly means only part of the word is used, with some letters taken away
united suggests letters joined up and merged, so what is left is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written before removing letters
as means like, in the sense of in the manner of

explanation.surface: Manchester United's bosses are compared to the two celebrated German football coaches.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer plus AS rearranges to the managers, so take AS out of the word and rearrange the rest. Some solvers instead join MAN and GER from inside the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Jürgen Klopp and Thomas Tuchel are both German nationals, so the question mark marks a definition by example.

clue.text: Second half for Exeter without end

indicators.note: the second half of a word means only its last three of six letters are used

blocks.note: the back half of the Devon city's name
minus means lacking or without

explanation.surface: A football commentary: Exeter City play the second half without a striker up front.
explanation.walkthrough: Exeter is a city in Devon with a League football club, which makes 'second half' read as the half of a match.
explanation.definitionFit: A terminus is the end of a railway or bus line, and more generally a final point or limit.

clue.text: A fan of Guy, not surprisingly

indicators.note: something that happens surprisingly comes out in an unexpected way, so these letters appear in an unexpected order

blocks.note: Guy is the setter, who refers to himself as I
taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: The setter Guy admits that his followers are, unsurprisingly, rare.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter often clues himself by his pseudonym, which here gives I. 'Not surprisingly' reads as an idiom but splits into fodder and indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: To be into something or someone is the informal way of saying you are keen on them, like an enthusiast.

clue.text: Taking no side in war, nervous about the end of it

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter only
about means going around, so one part wraps the other

blocks.note: neural means relating to the nerves
the final letter of this short word

explanation.surface: A country stays out of a conflict, anxious about how it will end.
explanation.definitionFit: A neutral nation keeps out of a war and takes the part of neither belligerent.

clue.text: About to be beaten, won't hero pester guards?

indicators.note: a phrase that guards something holds it inside, so the solution sits within these letters

blocks.note: read straight through the three words, ignoring the apostrophe and spaces

explanation.surface: Facing defeat, someone wonders why the hero won't harass the guards.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts at the second letter of won't and ends three letters into pester.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxer on the ropes is close to being knocked out, so the idiom means near to defeat.

clue.text: Time ship's fitter set off

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
a rigger fits a ship's ropes and sails

explanation.surface: The ship's fitter is late and the time has come for him to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: To trigger an alarm or an explosion is to set it off, to start it happening.

clue.text: Tell tot again

blocks.note: first meaning: to narrate or relate a story
second meaning: to add up the figures a second time, as in an election

explanation.surface: Someone tells a small child to go round once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tot' looks like a toddler but is the verb to tot up, to add.
explanation.definitionFit: To recount a tale is to narrate it; a re-count is a second tally of votes or numbers.

clue.text: Widow of a king potentially making a parent richer

indicators.note: potentially suggests what the letters could become once they are rearranged

blocks.note: thirteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Marrying a king could make a widowed parent wealthier.
explanation.definitionFit: Catherine Parr was the sixth wife of Henry VIII and outlived him, so she was a royal widow.

clue.text: One epitomising life after death?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who embodies an afterlife, a ghost or a believer in resurrection
setter's reading: a writer who summarises a person's life once they have died, in a newspaper

explanation.surface: A question about who best represents existence beyond the grave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Epitomising' looks like embodying, but here it means summing up briefly, and 'after death' is when the summary is written.
explanation.definitionFit: This journalist writes the death notices that sum up a person's career in print.

clue.text: Hearing Joey, perhaps wish otherwise

indicators.note: hearing means we go by what the ear takes in, not by spelling

blocks.note: a joey is a baby kangaroo, a roo

explanation.surface: Someone hearing a person called Joey wishes things had gone differently.
explanation.walkthrough: Joey looks like a name, but a joey is a young kangaroo; 'perhaps' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue something is to regret it, wishing it had happened otherwise.

clue.text: Waterfall swimmers must get up, a small one flowing quietly

indicators.note: flowing suggests letters running loose and settling in a new order

blocks.note: nine letters to rearrange
p, piano, is the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: Fish heading upstream must clear a small, gently running fall.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole first half: a waterfall that fish have to jump up.
explanation.definitionFit: A salmon leap is a weir or fall in a river which salmon must jump to reach their spawning grounds.

clue.text: Purposeless commercial break

blocks.note: an ad is a commercial
a rift is a break or split

explanation.surface: A pointless advertising interval on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial break' reads as one TV phrase; split it into two separate words.
explanation.definitionFit: To be adrift is to be without direction or aim, like a boat drifting loose.

clue.text: Pool user adjusted self-cleaning facility

indicators.note: adjusted means altered, so these letters are set in a different order

blocks.note: eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A swimmer has fixed the automatic cleaning system at the baths.
explanation.walkthrough: A superloo is a British term for an automated public toilet that washes itself after each use.
explanation.definitionFit: The facility, a public convenience, cleans itself automatically between users.

clue.text: A hundred lurk around small silent arcade

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
to loiter is to lurk about
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A crowd of people loiter about a small, hushed shopping arcade.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloister is a covered walkway around a monastery quadrangle, a quiet arched passage.

clue.text: Resort a beautiful stone city, with English moving in

indicators.note: a letter for English moves one place inward, so the word's letters end in a new order

blocks.note: marble is a prized decorative stone
LA, Los Angeles

explanation.surface: A Spanish resort is praised as a lovely stone-built town where English people are settling.
explanation.walkthrough: The E at the end of the stone moves one place in, before the L. Marbella, on the Costa del Sol, is famous for its English residents.
explanation.definitionFit: Marbella is a holiday town on Spain's southern coast, a Mediterranean beach destination.

clue.text: Step on a rope-ladder right next to field

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
at can mean beside, as in at the door
a line of work is a field

explanation.surface: Someone climbs a rope ladder alongside a meadow.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratlines are the small cross-ropes on a ship's shrouds, used as rungs for climbing the rigging.

clue.text: Spot solicitor outside in lane

indicators.note: the outside of a word is its first and last letters, leaving the middle behind

blocks.note: a pimp solicits clients on behalf of prostitutes
the first and last letters of this word

explanation.surface: A lawyer is spotted standing outside in the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solicitor' suggests a British lawyer, but here it is one who solicits on the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A pimple is a spot on the skin, a small inflamed swelling.

clue.text: Poor countryman hunted birds, saving hearts

indicators.note: saving means except for, so that letter is left out

blocks.note: game birds shot on shoots; the word serves as its own plural
H is the card-game abbreviation for hearts

explanation.surface: A poor farm labourer shot game birds but spared the ones that touched him.
explanation.definitionFit: A peasant is a poor smallholder or labourer working the land in the country.

clue.text: Peers rule out going back to basics

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter alone

blocks.note: to bar is to exclude or rule out
on as in a show that is going on
the final letter of this word

explanation.surface: Members of the Lords refuse to return to old-fashioned fundamentals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going back to basics' reads as one political slogan; it splits into on, then the tail of basics.
explanation.definitionFit: Barons are the lowest rank of the British peerage, so they are peers of the realm.

clue.text: Clear goal

blocks.note: first meaning: to make as profit after deductions
second meaning: the mesh frame a ball is struck into

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read like a football command to clear the ball from the goalmouth.
explanation.definitionFit: To net a sum is to clear it as profit; the net is the goal in football or hockey.

clue.text: Experimental hosts tonight having three parties

indicators.note: something that hosts takes another inside it as a guest

blocks.note: trial as an adjective, as in a trial run
later on today, as tonight is

explanation.surface: A cutting-edge venue is holding three separate parties this evening.
explanation.definitionFit: A trilateral agreement is one made between three sides, each a party to it.

clue.text: Discharged one day after a year

blocks.note: p.a., per annum, means a year
I is the Roman numeral for one
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone is released from hospital or prison a day after a full year inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists the parts in reverse; 'after' places the year first.
explanation.definitionFit: A debt that has been discharged has been settled, so it is paid.

clue.text: Obvious one's over depression

indicators.note: over in a down-or-across sense means turned over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: one's expanded as one has, which in the first person is I've
a dent is a small depression in a surface

explanation.surface: It is plain that someone has got over their low mood.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'one's' as 'one has', then as the speaker's I've; turned round it starts the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something evident is plain to see, clearly apparent to anyone.

clue.text: National anthem of Chad? Oddly, nothing

indicators.note: oddly means taking the first, third and fifth letters and dropping the rest

blocks.note: the odd-numbered letters of these two words
nada is Spanish slang for nothing

explanation.surface: Asked what Chad's anthem is, the answer is that there is none.
explanation.definitionFit: O Canada is the official national anthem of Canada.

clue.text: Victim's appeal heard

indicators.note: heard means the word is judged by its sound, not by how it is written

blocks.note: to pray is to appeal or plead

explanation.surface: A victim's plea for help is listened to in court.
explanation.definitionFit: Prey is a creature hunted by another, and by extension anyone who falls victim.

clue.text: Maybe Cherries scored, making one son dissatisfied

indicators.note: making one into son means the letter standing for one is replaced by the letter for son

blocks.note: cherries are an example of fruit, hence maybe
to rate is to score or grade

explanation.surface: Bournemouth, nicknamed the Cherries, scored, leaving a fan's son unhappy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cherries is the nickname of AFC Bournemouth, an English football club, but here they are just fruit; the I (one) in it becomes S (son).
explanation.definitionFit: Someone frustrated feels thwarted and discontent because their aims are blocked.
